name: cross product

functions.name: texp
functions.body: if numberp(x) and x<0 then concat("\\left(",tex1(x),"\\right)") else tex1(x)

functions.name: texsumf
functions.body: block([L:first(args(e))], concat(tex1(first(L)), apply(sconcat, map(lambda([t], concat("+",texp(t))), rest(L)))))

functions.name: texnsum
functions.body: block([L:first(args(e))], concat(tex1(first(L)), apply(sconcat, map(lambda([t], if numberp(t) and t<0 then concat("-",tex1(-t)) else concat("+",tex1(t))), rest(L)))))

functions.name: cft
functions.body: concat(if c<0 then "-" else (if fst then "" else "+"), if abs(c)=1 then "" else tex1(abs(c)), tex1(s))

functions.name: texlin
functions.body: block([L:args(e), out:"", f:true], for k:1 thru length(L) step 2 do (if L[k]#0 then (out:concat(out, cft(L[k],L[k+1],f)), f:false)), if out="" then "0" else out)

questiontext:
Unlike the scalar product, the vector product (or cross product) \(u \times v\) of two vectors \(u,v \in R^3\) is a vector! The formula for the vector product of two vectors is given below together with an easy way to remember this formula. The easy way involves an abuse of notation: We write the vector product as a determinant where the entries of the first row are not numbers but rather the vectors of the standard basis for \(R^3\), namely \(i,j,k\).

\[{{CT:0}} \times {{CT:1}} = \det\left({{CT:2}}\right) = {{CT:3}}\]

Let us review the basic properties of the cross product:

  1. Linearity in the first vector (and similarly in the second one): \( (av+bu) \times w = a v \times w + b u \times w, \quad \forall a,b \in R, u,v,w \in R^3 \).
  2. Anti Symmetry: \( v \times w = - w \times v, \quad \forall v,w \in R^3\).
  3. \(v \times w = 0\) if and only if \(\{v,w\}\) are linearly dependent.
  4. \(v \times w \) is orthogonal to both \(v\) and \(w\). Hence it is orthogonal to the plane \(Span\{v,w\}\).
  5. The length of this vector \(||v \times w|| = ||v|| ||w|| \sin(\theta)\) where \(\theta\) is the angle between the two vectors. Geometrically this number is the area of the parallelogram spanned by \(v\) and \(w\). See the figure below.
  6. When \(\{v,w\}\) are linearly independent (i.e. when \(v \times w \ne 0\)) then \(v,w,v\times w\) is a positively oriented triplet of vectors. This last rule determines, which of the two vectors satisfying (4) and (5) above is \(v\times w\).

a

Please calculate the cross product:

\(v \times w = {{CT:4}} \times {{CT:5}} =\) [[input:ans1]]
[[validation:ans1]]

How to enter: each entry in its own box: a number, a fraction (e.g. 1/2) or an expression (e.g. sqrt(2)).

b

What is the area of the triangle whose vertices are the origin and the two vectors appearing in the cross product above.

Area = [[input:ans2]]
[[validation:ans2]]
generalfeedback:
Outline: The cross product is computed component by component from the determinant formula. The area of the triangle is half the area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors, which is the length of the cross product.
Step 1 — The cross product (part a)
Put the components of the two vectors under the unit vectors and expand along the first row:

\[ v\times w=\det\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {{CT:6}} & {{CT:7}} & {{CT:8}} \\ {{CT:9}} & {{CT:10}} & {{CT:11}} \end{pmatrix} \]

Writing \(v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)\), \(w=(w_1,w_2,w_3)\), the components are

\[ \begin{aligned} (v\times w)_1 &= v_2w_3-v_3w_2 = {{CT:12}}-{{CT:13}} = {{CT:14}} = {{CT:15}} \\ (v\times w)_2 &= v_3w_1-v_1w_3 = {{CT:16}}-{{CT:17}} = {{CT:18}} = {{CT:19}} \\ (v\times w)_3 &= v_1w_2-v_2w_1 = {{CT:20}}-{{CT:21}} = {{CT:22}} = {{CT:23}} \end{aligned} \]

Hence

\[ v\times w={{CT:24}} \]

Step 2 — The area of the triangle (part b)
The area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors is the length of the cross product, \(||v\times w||=||v||\,||w||\sin\theta\), and the triangle is half of the parallelogram (a diagonal cuts it into two congruent triangles). The length of the cross product is

\[ ||v\times w||=\sqrt{{{CT:25}}}=\sqrt{ {{CT:26}} } \]

Hence the area of the triangle is[[if test="{{CT:32}}"]]

\[ \text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{ {{CT:26}} }=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {{CT:27}}={{CT:28}} \]

[[elif test="{{CT:33}}"]]

\[ \text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{ {{CT:26}} }=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{ {{CT:29}}\cdot {{CT:30}} }=\sqrt{ {{CT:30}} } \]

[[elif test="{{CT:34}}"]]

\[ \text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{ {{CT:26}} }=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{ {{CT:29}}\cdot {{CT:30}} }={{CT:31}}\sqrt{ {{CT:30}} } \]

[[else]]

\[ \text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{ {{CT:26}} } \]

[[/if]]

on_true.feedback: Part a — correct. Your cross product is correct.

on_false.feedback:
Part a — incorrect. The correct calculation is as follows:

\[ {{CT:4}} \times {{CT:5}} = {@a1@} = {{CT:24}} \]

on_true.feedback: Part b — correct. Your area calculation is correct.
Part b — incorrect. You did the correct calculation for the area, but using the wrong value you got previously for the cross product.
Part b — incorrect. This is the area of the parallelogram. The area of the triangle is exactly half of that.
Part b — incorrect. An area can never be negative!
